## Epidemic modelling workflow

```{julia}
#| label: fig-s-p01-pipeline
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "A connected modelling workflow from surveillance data to intervention decisions."
using CairoMakie, EpiModelingCourse

# A schematic drawn in a 0-100 square: boxes, elbow connectors, arrowheads.
palette = course_palette()

const FIGURE_HEIGHT = 430
const CONNECTOR = (:grey45, 0.9)
const DESCRIPTOR = :grey35

outcomes = [
    (85, palette.susceptible, "Simulate",
        "deterministic · stochastic ·\nindividual-based models"),
    (62, palette.incidence, "Infer",
        "observation models · calibration ·\nBayesian inference · identifiability"),
    (39, palette.recovered, "Compare scenarios",
        "alternative assumptions · uncertainty ·\nintervention strategies"),
    (16, palette.infected, "Design interventions",
        "objectives · constraints · optimisation"),
]

# Font sizes are pixels and box geometry is in data units, so convert one to the
# other and stack the lines from the top of a vertically centred block.
line_height(fontsize) = fontsize * 100 / FIGURE_HEIGHT * 1.25
line_count(text) = count(==('\n'), text) + 1

function box!(ax, cx, cy, w, h, colour, entries; gap = 1.0)
    poly!(ax, Rect2f(cx - w / 2, cy - h / 2, w, h);
        color = :white, strokecolor = colour, strokewidth = 2)
    heights = [line_count(text) * line_height(fontsize)
               for (text, fontsize, _) in entries]
    y = cy + (sum(heights) + gap * (length(entries) - 1)) / 2
    for ((text, fontsize, textcolour), height) in zip(entries, heights)
        text!(ax, cx, y; text, align = (:center, :top), fontsize,
            font = textcolour === colour ? :bold : :regular, color = textcolour)
        y -= height + gap
    end
    return nothing
end

# Arrowheads are markers rather than arrow plots: the connectors are elbows,
# so only the final segment needs a head.
head!(ax, x, y) = scatter!(ax, [x], [y];
    marker = :rtriangle, markersize = 13, color = CONNECTOR)

with_theme(course_theme()) do
    fig = Figure(size = (960, FIGURE_HEIGHT))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, 1])
    hidedecorations!(ax)
    hidespines!(ax)
    limits!(ax, 0, 100, 0, 100)

    box!(ax, 8, 50, 14, 20, :grey35, [("Surveillance\ndata", 15, :grey35)])
    box!(ax, 30, 50, 26, 26, :grey20,
        [("Modelling workflow", 19, :grey20),
         ("data · model code · algorithms", 12, DESCRIPTOR)])
    for (cy, colour, title, descriptor) in outcomes
        box!(ax, 66, cy, 32, 19, colour,
            [(title, 17, colour), (descriptor, 12, DESCRIPTOR)])
    end
    box!(ax, 93, 50, 12, 20, :grey35, [("Intervention\ndecision", 15, :grey35)])

    ys = [cy for (cy, _, _, _) in outcomes]

    # Data into the model.
    lines!(ax, [15.0, 17.2], [50.0, 50.0]; color = CONNECTOR, linewidth = 2)
    head!(ax, 17.6, 50)

    # The workflow fans out to the four tasks.
    lines!(ax, [43.0, 46.5], [50.0, 50.0]; color = CONNECTOR, linewidth = 2)
    lines!(ax, [46.5, 46.5], [minimum(ys), maximum(ys)]; color = CONNECTOR, linewidth = 2)
    for cy in ys
        lines!(ax, [46.5, 49.2], [cy, cy]; color = CONNECTOR, linewidth = 2)
        head!(ax, 49.6, cy)
    end

    # The four tasks merge into one decision.
    for cy in ys
        lines!(ax, [82.0, 85.0], [cy, cy]; color = CONNECTOR, linewidth = 2)
    end
    lines!(ax, [85.0, 85.0], [minimum(ys), maximum(ys)]; color = CONNECTOR, linewidth = 2)
    lines!(ax, [85.0, 86.6], [50.0, 50.0]; color = CONNECTOR, linewidth = 2)
    head!(ax, 87.0, 50)

    fig
end
```

::: {.notes}
Calibration and Bayesian inference are not sessions, and the
programme points at the LSHTM course "Model Fitting and Inference for Infectious Disease Dynamics" instead. Identifiability sits in this box because it asks what the data could tell you about the parameters, and that half is taught. The observation-model, parameter-estimation and Bayesian-inference chapters are written and available for self-study, the interventions session makes the connection in passing because the optimiser that finds the best intervention is the same machinery that finds the best-fitting parameters.
:::

## What we want when modelling? {.smaller}

::: {style="margin-top: 3.5em;"}

| What we want | What Julia offers |
|---|---|
| Models that are easy to inspect and modify | Scientific models written as ordinary Julia code |
| Thousands of simulations and scenarios | Compiled performance |
| Simulation, fitting and intervention analysis | Tools designed to work together in one language |
| Analyses that colleagues can reproduce | Recorded packages, versions and random seeds |
:::

::: {.notes}

:::

## Can't we do the same in other languages? {.smaller}

::: {style="margin-top: 1.5em;"}
Yes you can. Comparable models can be built, simulated and fitted in R, Python and
elsewhere. The methods are not unique to Julia.

What Julia brings together:

- Model code can remain generic. Multiple dispatch selects an applicable method from the argument types, and those types give the compiler information it can use to optimise execution.
- Julia’s scientific packages make use of shared types and interfaces. This often allows a problem specification to be reused with compatible solvers and embedded in sensitivity, optimisation and inference workflows.

Together, these features can mean less duplicated model code and less
framework-specific integration code when moving between stages of an analysis.

:::
::: {.notes}
None of these tasks is unique to Julia. R and Python can also support epidemic modelling. Julia becomes particularly attractive when we are developing a custom model and need to run it repeatedly. The code describing transmission can remain readable Julia code, while Julia compiles it for efficient execution. We can then connect that model to simulation, fitting, uncertainty analysis and intervention design without maintaining a separate low-level implementation.
:::

## If you are interested in performance...

These serial microbenchmarks compare implementations of the same small numerical algorithms.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-s-p01-benchmarks
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Run time relative to C on the JuliaLang micro-benchmark suite: grey points are individual benchmarks, the large point is their geometric mean. Data: JuliaLang/Microbenchmarks, 2022."
using CSV, DataFrames, CairoMakie, EpiModelingCourse

const BENCH_DIR = joinpath(pkgdir(EpiModelingCourse), "data")
geomean(x) = exp(sum(log, x) / length(x))
pretty_name = Dict("c" => "C", "julia" => "Julia", "lua" => "LuaJIT",
    "fortran" => "Fortran", "java" => "Java", "javascript" => "JavaScript",
    "matlab" => "Matlab", "mathematica" => "Mathematica", "python" => "Python",
    "octave" => "Octave", "r" => "R", "rust" => "Rust", "go" => "Go")
language_colour(l) = l == "julia" ? :firebrick : l == "c" ? :steelblue : :grey35

# Times as a multiple of C, over the benchmarks C itself ran.
function relative_to_c(table)
    ctime = Dict(r.benchmark => r.time for r in eachrow(table[table.language .== "c", :]))
    kept = table[[haskey(ctime, r.benchmark) for r in eachrow(table)], :]
    kept.rel = [r.time / ctime[r.benchmark] for r in eachrow(kept)]
    return kept
end

bench22 = relative_to_c(CSV.read(joinpath(BENCH_DIR, "language_benchmarks_2022.csv"), DataFrame))
summary22 = sort!(combine(groupby(bench22, :language), :rel => geomean => :gmean), :gmean)
order = summary22.language
position = Dict(l => i for (i, l) in enumerate(order))

with_theme(course_theme()) do
    fig = Figure(size = (960, 450))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; yscale = log10, ylabel = "run time / C time",
        xticks = (1:length(order), [pretty_name[l] for l in order]),
        xticklabelrotation = pi / 6, xticklabelsize = 19, yticklabelsize = 18,
        ylabelsize = 21)
    hlines!(ax, [1.0]; color = (:black, 0.35), linestyle = :dash)
    scatter!(ax, [position[r.language] for r in eachrow(bench22)], bench22.rel;
        color = (:grey70, 0.55), markersize = 9)
    scatter!(ax, 1:length(order), summary22.gmean;
        color = [language_colour(l) for l in order], markersize = 21)
    fig
end
```

- Julia's geometric-mean runtime is about **1.2× C** in this snapshot.
- It does not predict the speed of every application.
- It does show that custom numerical loops need not be rewritten in a
  lower-level language.

::: {.notes}
These are micro-benchmarks: small tasks such as recursive Fibonacci, integer parsing and the Mandelbrot set. The benchmark documentation says so itself, that these are not comprehensive application benchmarks, and that they test common language patterns using serial implementations. 
The vertical axis is logarithmic, so each gridline is a factor of ten, and the grey points show that a single language spans a wide range across tasks. Data from the JuliaLang Microbenchmarks repository, 2022; the ordering has been stable for years, but present the values as a snapshot rather than a current measurement.
Why this matters here: epidemic models are run thousands of times over, in ensembles, sensitivity sweeps and inference, so the cost of the inner loop is not an abstract concern.
:::

## If you are interested in code size...

```{julia}
#| label: fig-s-p01-codelength
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Run time against source length for the same benchmark suite, one point per language. Data from 2016, which is the last year source lengths were published with the timings."
bench16 = relative_to_c(CSV.read(joinpath(BENCH_DIR, "language_benchmarks_2016.csv"), DataFrame))
summary16 = combine(groupby(bench16, :language),
    :rel => geomean => :gmean, :kb => first => :kb)
label_left = ("c", "fortran", "java", "python", "r")

with_theme(course_theme()) do
    fig = Figure(size = (960, 450))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; yscale = log10, xlabel = "source length (KB)",
        ylabel = "run time / C time", xlabelsize = 21, ylabelsize = 21,
        xticklabelsize = 18, yticklabelsize = 18)
    scatter!(ax, summary16.kb, summary16.gmean;
        color = [language_colour(l) for l in summary16.language], markersize = 17)
    text!(ax, summary16.kb, summary16.gmean;
        text = [pretty_name[l] for l in summary16.language],
        align = [(l in label_left ? :right : :left, :center) for l in summary16.language],
        offset = [(l in label_left ? -13 : 13, 0) for l in summary16.language],
        fontsize = 17, color = [language_colour(l) for l in summary16.language])
    xlims!(ax, 2.0, 13.0)
    ylims!(ax, 0.7, 700)
    fig
end
```

::: {.notes}
This is the older figure, 2016, because source lengths stopped being published alongside the timings after that. Nothing since has moved Julia out of that corner, but present it as a historical snapshot. Both axes matter: languages on the left are compact, languages at the bottom are fast, and before Julia you generally chose one or the other. 
:::

## Finding your way around VS Code {.smaller}

::: {style="margin-top: 2.5em;"}
| Where | What you will use it for |
|---|---|
| *Explorer*, left | the course folder — open the *folder*, not a single file |
| *Editor*, centre | the `.qmd` worksheet you are working in |
| *Panel*, bottom | the Julia REPL and the terminal, as tabs |
| *Plot pane* | figures, appears when the first one is drawn |

- The command palette, `Cmd`/`Ctrl`+`Shift`+`P`, reaches everything:
  *Julia: Start REPL*, *Quarto: Render*.
- The folder you open is how Julia and Quarto know which project you are in.

:::
::: {.notes}
Show this live rather than reading it: open the folder, start the REPL from the
palette, run one cell, let the plot pane appear.

Coming from RStudio, two things are different and both cause the same confusion.
RStudio has four fixed panes; VS Code shows whatever is open, so the REPL is not
there until you start it. And RStudio's menus are replaced by the command
palette, which is worth demonstrating once because it is how they will find
anything they cannot see.

The failure that costs the most time is opening a single file instead of the
folder. Julia and Quarto both take the open folder as the project, so a worksheet
opened on its own will not find the course environment. If someone reports a
missing package, check this before anything else, together with the environment
name at the `pkg>` prompt.
:::

## The REPL has four modes {.smaller}

REPL stands for Read, Evaluate, Print, and Loop

Type one character at an empty prompt; `Backspace` returns.

| Key | Mode | For |
|---|---|---|
| — | Julia | evaluating expressions (default) |
| `?` | help | `?expm1` — docstring, signatures, examples |
| `]` | package | `]st`, `]instantiate` — and it names the active environment |
| `;` | shell | `ls`, `cd`, `git status` without leaving Julia |

- The package prompt names the **active environment** — check it first when a
  package seems missing. Start Julia with `--project=.` from the repo root.

::: {.notes}
Demonstrate the four modes live rather than reading the table: enter and leave
each one, and show `?expm1` in particular, since help mode answers most "what
arguments does this take" questions faster than a web search and works offline.
Point out the environment name in the package prompt, which the next slide picks
up: a package that appears to be missing almost always means the project
environment was never activated, and a plain `julia` starts in the default
environment wherever it is launched.
:::

## Your environment

::: {style="margin-top: 1.5em;"}
- `Project.toml` — the packages this project asks for.
- `Manifest.toml` — the exact version of every package resolved.
- `Pkg.instantiate()` rebuilds that set anywhere. You ran it in setup.
- The `pkg>` prompt names your environment. "Not installed" usually means "not here".

:::
::: {.notes}
If someone hits a package error today it is almost certainly the environment, not the installation: a bare `julia` starts in the default environment wherever it is launched, so the fix is `--project=.` from the repository root, or `] activate .`. The setup page has this under "a package seems to be missing". Worth saying plainly what the Manifest adds: it pins the resolved version of every package rather than naming the packages. R has renv, so this is not a Julia exclusive. The difference is that project and manifest environments are part of Julia's standard package workflow rather than an add-on.
:::

## Julia code can stay close to the mathematics {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
Force of infection:

$$
\lambda = \beta c \frac{I}{N}
$$

Compartmental rates:

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}S}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\lambda S
$$

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} = \lambda S - \gamma I
$$

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}R}{\mathrm{d}t} = \gamma I
$$
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
```julia
function sir_ode!(du, u, (; β, c, γ, N), t)
    S, I, R = u

    λ = β * c * I / N

    du[1] = -λ * S
    du[2] =  λ * S - γ * I
    du[3] =  γ * I
    return nothing
end
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.6em;"}
| | |
|---|---|
| $\beta$ | transmission probability per contact |
| $c$ | contacts per person per day |
| $\gamma$ | recovery rate, per day |
| $N$ | population size, $S + I + R$ |
:::

::: {style="margin-top: 1em;"}
- Greek letters are ordinary variable names: `\beta`⇥ → `β`, `\gamma`⇥ → `γ`, `\lambda`⇥ → `λ`. Plain ASCII names works as well.
:::
:::

:::
::: {.notes}
The point is that you can read the implementation against the equations line by line, which is how you check a model you did not write.

This is not a Julia distinction. R allows non-ASCII identifiers in a UTF-8 locale, and Python has allowed them since PEP 3131, so
this is not a capability other languages lack. What Julia adds is that the LaTeX-style tab completion is built into the REPL and the editor tooling, and that the convention is common enough that package APIs use these names themselves. It is a readability and convention argument, not a composability one.
:::

## Broadcasting: the dot {.smaller}

Broadcasting allows to perform operations elementwise, and can be called implicitly by "dot" operations. For example:
```{julia}
#| label: s-p01-broadcast
#| echo: true
cases = [12, 40, 7]
pop   = [1000, 5000, 800]

per_100k = 1e5 .* cases ./ pop
```

Or to functions like:

```{julia}
#| label: s-p02-broadcast
#| echo: true
incidence_per_100k(case_count, population) =
    100_000 * case_count / population

cases      = [12, 40, 7]
populations = [1000, 5000, 800]

per_100k = incidence_per_100k.(cases, populations)
```

::: {.notes}
In many languages you vectorise because loops are slow, so the vectorised form is forced on you whether or not it expresses the model clearly. Here a loop compiles to the same thing, so broadcasting is a choice about readability. That matters most when a mechanism does not vectorise neatly: you can write it as ordinary scalar code and loops
without paying for it.
:::

## In place: `!` and `.=` {.smaller}

::: {style="margin-top: 2.5em;"}
```{julia}
#| label: s-p01-inplace
#| echo: true

function incidence_per_100k!(out, cases, populations)
    out .= incidence_per_100k.(cases, populations)
    return nothing
end

out = zeros(length(cases))

incidence_per_100k!(out, cases, populations)

out == per_100k  
```

- The `!` signals that the function modifies an argument
- `.=` computes and writes each element directly into the existing `out` array
- The result is stored in `out`, not returned. Solvers can reuse this array across repeated calls, avoiding a new output array each time
:::
::: {.notes}
The `!` signals that the function modifies an argument, and `.=` computes and writes each element directly into the existing `out` array. The result is stored in `out`, not returned. Solvers can reuse this array across repeated calls, avoiding a new output array each time.
:::

## Named tuples and multiple dispatch {.smaller}

::: {style="margin-top: 2.5em;"}
```{julia}
#| label: s-p01-dispatch
#| echo: true
p = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0)   # read by name, never by position

force_of_infection(p, I::Number)         = p.β * p.c * I / p.N
force_of_infection(p, I::AbstractVector) = p.β .* p.c .* I ./ p.N

(force_of_infection(p, 10), force_of_infection(p, [10, 50, 200]))
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.6em;"}
| Call                                   | Method selected     |
| -------------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| `force_of_infection(p, 10)`            | `I::Number`         |
| `force_of_infection(p, [10, 50, 200])` | `I::AbstractVector` |
:::

- Both definitions are methods of the same function. Julia selects the applicable method from the positional argument types
- The type of `I` determines whether the scalar or vector method is used

:::
::: {.notes}
On the named tuple, the failure worth naming is the quiet one. A positional parameter tuple that someone reorders still runs, and returns wrong numbers with no error. Reading by field cannot fail that way. Part A of the worksheet asks them to think about exactly this.

On dispatch, the example is built so the *second* argument decides, because the habit from other languages is to expect the first argument, or a receiver object, to own the behaviour. It does not here. That is what lets a solver package written by one group and a problem type written by another meet without either importing the other's opinions, which is the second bullet on the "can we do the same in other languages" slide.

Resist teaching the type system. The one consequence they need today is that `solve(prob, Tsit5())` needs no glue code, so handing the same model to a different algorithm, a sensitivity package or an inference package later leaves the model untouched. The ODE session demonstrates it on a real problem, so today it is enough to assert.
:::

## Reproducible randomness {.smaller}

::: {style="margin-top: 2.5em;"}
```{julia}
#| label: s-p01-rng
#| echo: true

using StableRNGs

seed = 123

draws_a = rand(StableRNG(seed), 1)
draws_b = rand(StableRNG(seed), 1)
draws_c = rand(StableRNG(seed + 1), 1)

println("draws_a == draws_b: ", draws_a == draws_b)
println("draws_a != draws_c: ", draws_a != draws_c)
println("draws_a: ", draws_a, " draws_b: ", draws_b, " draws_c: ", draws_c)
```

- A random-number generator produces a sequence
- The seed determines where that sequence starts 
- Recreating `StableRNG(123)` reproduces the same draws
- The generator advances when it is used, so another call using the same generator produces the next values in the sequence
:::

::: {.notes}
The contrast worth drawing is with a global seed. `StableRNGs` fixes the stream
across Julia versions, where the built-in generator may legitimately change
between releases, which is why every stochastic figure in this course reproduces.
Passing the generator as an argument also makes the source of randomness visible
at the call site instead of depending on whatever ran before it.
:::
